title: Dedication
hook: giving away the merit of every practice to all beings

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four great vows: beings without number, delusions without end, and a promise made anyway. Your line: numberless, I vow. What small piece of something too big did you do? Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

Someone has spent an afternoon copying a sutra by hand, line after careful line, the ink still drying. Whatever good came from it, it's theirs. They earned it. And then, before the brush is washed, they give it away. In Mahayana practice the last words of a session can be words that aren't about the one who practiced at all. They send the good of it out the door, to everyone. Today: dedication.
screen: `AN AFTERNOON OF COPYING.` → `THE GOOD IS THEIRS.` → `GIVE IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, the thing being given. Buddhists speak of merit, punya in Sanskrit, puñña in Pali: the good that comes from a good act. Giving, keeping a precept, sitting, chanting, each leaves something behind, like warmth in a room after a fire. The old teaching says good acts bear good fruit. Merit is the name for that fruit while it ripens. Second, the turn. In Mahayana practice, merit isn't kept. At the close of a sit or a ceremony, people recite a dedication, turning the merit toward the awakening of all beings. The Sanskrit word is parinamana, often given in English as turning over. The bodhisattva works for the sake of all, so even the fruit of the work goes to all. Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva closes with a whole chapter of it: may the good of this go here, and there, and to every being in pain. Third, a neighbor inside the same house. Theravada Buddhists share merit too. After a meal offered to monks, or a chant for someone who has died, a family may pour water slowly from one vessel into another while the monks recite verses, and the merit is shared with the dead and with all beings. Different schools, different words, the same open hand. Fourth, the strange arithmetic. You might think merit given away is merit lost. Some teachers in this tradition say the opposite: a lamp that lights another lamp isn't dimmed. Whether that's taken literally or not, the practice does something plain. It ends the session facing outward. The last thought isn't how did I do. It's who else is this for. Practice that ends that way is harder to turn into a scoreboard, and easier to carry into a kitchen, an office, a hard phone call.
screen: `MERIT: THE FRUIT OF A GOOD ACT.` · `TURNED TOWARD ALL BEINGS.` · `WATER POURED, MERIT SHARED.` · `A LAMP LIGHTING A LAMP.` · then, large: `GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: dedicate this sit. Settle, and breathe. For the next two minutes, just sit, the way you have on other days. Nothing special. Then, near the end, before the bell, think of whatever steadiness or quiet this sit gave you, even a little. And send it out. To someone you love. To someone you don't know. To someone who's having a harder day than you. If you have words from your own tradition for this, you can say them. If not, the intention is enough. Then let the bell close it. The bell holds the time.
Dedication. Parinamana, turning the merit of a practice toward all beings, so the good of it doesn't stay with the one who did it. Today's word.

Your line: given away. Today, when you finish something you're proud of, take one breath and turn its good toward someone else before you take the credit. Tomorrow, the book honored. Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Mahayana communities close a sit, chant or ceremony with a dedication of merit to all beings; in Theravada communities merit is shared too, sometimes while water is poured from one vessel into another as monks recite verses.

pairs: merit, the fruit of a good act

myth: dedicating merit is only a Mahayana practice
Theravada Buddhists share merit too, with the dead and with all beings.
in Mahayana, the merit of a practice is kept by the one who practiced
it is turned over, dedicated to the awakening of all beings.
Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva closes with a dedication
its last chapter turns the good of the whole work toward every being.

fork.setup: you've just finished a long sit and it went well. the session isn't over yet. what comes last?
options: turn its good toward all beings
set a longer goal for tomorrow
fork.reveal: in Mahayana practice the last words dedicate the merit to all beings, so the session ends facing outward.

original.note: Sanskrit: turning over, the dedication of merit to others.

trapdoor: what you thought: dedication means sticking with something.
what it means: in Buddhist practice it's giving away the merit of what you just did, to all beings.
what a scholar hears: parinamana, turning merit toward awakening; Shantideva gives it a whole closing chapter, and Theravada shares merit too.
